lesson.title: Leaving Blanks to Fill In: What Parameters Are
lesson.summary: Parameters are the named placeholders listed in a function's definition that stand in for values the function will receive each time it is called.
lesson.body:
When you write def greet(name):, the word name inside the parentheses is a parameter: a placeholder name that the function's body can refer to, standing in for whatever value will actually be supplied when the function gets called. Parameters exist because a function defined once, like greet, needs to work correctly for many different inputs, not just one hardcoded value. Writing the body around a parameter name instead of a specific piece of data is what lets the same block of code produce "Hello, Amara!" for one call and "Hello, Diego!" for another, without changing a single line of the function definition itself.

A function can list more than one parameter, separated by commas, and the order in which they appear in the definition matters. Consider def rectangle_area(width, height): return width * height. Here width and height are two separate parameters. When this function is called, the values supplied are matched to these parameters by position, left to right, so the first value given becomes width and the second becomes height. rectangle_area(4, 9) computes width as 4 and height as 9, returning 4 * 9, which is 36. Swap the order of the call to rectangle_area(9, 4) and you still get 36 in this particular case, since multiplication does not care about order, but with def describe_rect(width, height): return str(width) + " by " + str(height), calling describe_rect(4, 9) produces '4 by 9' while describe_rect(9, 4) produces '9 by 4', a clearly different result, which shows why parameter order is not just a stylistic detail but something that can change what the function actually computes.

Parameters exist only inside the function that declares them. Once execution jumps into rectangle_area, width and height are usable names, but as soon as the function returns and control passes back out, those names disappear; they cannot be looked up anywhere outside that function's body. This is a direct consequence of how a function call works: each call creates its own fresh binding of parameter names to values, and that binding is torn down once the call finishes, which is also why two different calls, like square(5) and square(9), never interfere with each other even though both use the same parameter name n internally.

It helps to be precise about the vocabulary here, since parameters and arguments are easy to conflate, even though they describe two sides of the same relationship. The parameter is the name written in the function definition, the placeholder waiting to be filled. The value actually supplied at call time is called an argument, a distinction covered in detail next. For now, the key idea to hold onto is that parameters are what make a function's body generic: by writing return width * height instead of return 4 * 9, the function rectangle_area works correctly for every rectangle you will ever ask it about, not just one specific 4 by 9 rectangle, which is precisely the reusability that makes defining a function worth the effort in the first place.
